content: Garden angelica, scientifically known as Angelica archangelica (with synonyms such as Archangelica officinalis Hoffm and Archangelica officinalis var. himalaica C.B. Clarke), is a biennial plant belonging to the Apiaceae family, commonly referred to as the umbelliferous family. It is also known by alternative names such as Holy Ghost, Wild Celery, and Norwegian Angelica. During its first year of growth, the plant produces only leaves. In its second year, it develops a fluted stem that can grow up to two meters (approximately six feet) in height. The leaves are composed of numerous small leaflets, which are divided into three main groups, each of which is further subdivided into three smaller groups. The edges of these leaflets are finely serrated or toothed. The flowers of the plant bloom in July and are small, numerous, and yellowish or greenish in color. These flowers are arranged in large, globular umbels, which later produce pale yellow, oblong fruits. Garden angelica thrives in damp soil, particularly in areas near rivers or water deposits. It is important to distinguish this plant from the toxic Pastinaca sativa (commonly known as Wild Parsnip). Angelica archangelica grows naturally in northern regions of countries such as Finland, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Greenland, the Faroe Islands, and Iceland. It is also cultivated in France, particularly in the Marais Poitevin, a marshy region near Niort in the Deux-Sèvres department. Historically, garden angelica has been cultivated as both a vegetable and a medicinal plant since the 10th century. It gained significant popularity in Scandinavia during the 12th century and remains an integral part of Sami culture. The hollow stem of the plant can be fashioned into a flute-like instrument that produces a clarinet-like sound, likely used as a toy for children. The renowned botanist Linnaeus documented that the Sami people utilized angelica in reindeer milk. The plant has various culinary applications. It is used as a spice and to flavor liqueurs and spirits such as Chartreuse, Bénédictine, Vermouth, and Dubonnet. It is also used in omelets, trout dishes, and jams. The long, bright green stems are often candied and used as decorative elements. In Persian cuisine, the petals of angelica are incorporated into the spice mixture Advieh, which is used to flavor rice dishes, as well as chicken and bean-based recipes. Garden angelica is unique among the Umbelliferae family due to its pervasive aromatic odor, which is distinct from the scents of fennel, parsley, anise, caraway, or chervil. Some historical accounts compare its fragrance to musk, while others liken it to juniper. Even the roots of the plant are fragrant and are considered one of the principal aromatic substances of European origin. Although the other parts of the plant share the same flavor, their active components are thought to be more perishable. The plant contains a variety of bioactive compounds with medicinal properties. Chewing on angelica or consuming tea brewed from it can induce local anesthesia while simultaneously enhancing the immune system. Scientific studies have demonstrated its efficacy against various bacterial, fungal, and even viral infections. The essential oil extracted from the roots of Angelica archangelica contains β-terebangelene (C10H16) and other terpenes. The oil derived from the seeds also contains β-terebangelene, along with methylethylacetic acid and hydroxymyristic acid. Both the seeds and roots of angelica are occasionally used in the production of absinthe. The name Archangelica is derived from the Greek word arkhangelos, meaning archangel, based on the legend that the angel Gabriel revealed its medicinal uses. The plant is known by various names in different languages: in Finnish, it is called väinönputki; in Sami, it is referred to as fádnu, boska, or rássi; in German, it is arznei-engelwurz; in Dutch, grote engelwortel; in Farsi, gol-par; in Swedish, kvanne; in Norwegian, kvann; in Danish, kvan; and in Icelandic, it is called hvönn.
